Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care 
Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated 
Exchanges Proposed Rule 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
The American Diabetes Association (ADA) wishes to provide comments in response to 
the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule.1 We 
continue to be considered about the use of prior authorization and step therapy by health 
plans and believe that these practices have delayed necessary, and in some cases, 
lifesaving treatments and medications for people with diabetes, prediabetes, and obesity. 
While we appreciate CMSâ€™s attempt to streamline prior authorization processes, we urge 
CMS to go further and reduce the number of services and medications subject to prior 
authorization and eliminate the use of step therapy in Medicare.  
 
About ADA 
 
The ADA is a nationwide, nonprofit, voluntary health organization founded in 1940 and 
made up of individuals with diabetes, healthcare professionals who treat people with 
diabetes, research scientists, and other concerned individuals. The ADAâ€™s mission is to 
prevent and cure diabetes and to improve the lives of all people affected by diabetes. The 
ADA, the largest non-governmental organization that deals with the treatment and impact 
of diabetes, represents the 136 million individuals living with diabetes and prediabetes. 
 
1 Fed Reg. Vol. 91. April 14. 2026. 19890. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-04-14/pdf/2026-
07205.pdf. 
 
 
2451 Crystal Drive, Suite 900 
 
 
Arlington, VA 22202 
1-800-DIABETES (800-342-2383) 
 
 
The ADA also reviews and authors the most authoritative and widely followed clinical 
practice recommendations, guidelines, and standards for the treatment of diabetes2 and 
publishes the most influential professional journals concerning diabetes research and 
treatment. 
 
ADA Overarching Concerns on Prior Authorization 
 
Prior authorization can delay or inhibit the ability for people with diabetes to receive 
services, drugs, and devices that their physicians believe are most effective for the 
treatment of their conditions. Delays in accessing that treatment can cause irreparable 
patient harm, including disease progression, as well as physician apathy to prior 
authorization protocols, which are applied inconsistently across different payers, making 
it almost impossible to establish uniform systems and processes to handle all prior 
authorization requests. Further, the guidelines and medical necessity criteria of which 
these prior authorization standards are based, often go beyond existing federal 
guidelines and requirements. Insurance coverage and formulary decisions must be 
based on clinical evidence and the direction of health care providersâ€”and health 
plans should be required to use uniform standards and criteria.  
 
Patients must be protected and have avenues to push back against denied requests. 
Many patients simply are not appealing denied requests since they may not know how 
to or have the resources to do so. According to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF), 
nearly 53 million prior authorization requests were submitted to Medicare Advantage 
(MA) plans in 2024. MA plans denied or partially denied 4.1 million (7.7%) of these 
requests. Only 11.5% of denied prior authorization requests were appealed, but MA 
plans approved 80.7% of the appealed requests.3 These alarming statistics effectively 
mean that most requests should not have been denied in the first place, but since only a 
fraction of beneficiaries are appealing, the majority of requests remain denied, leaving 
patients without access to vital services and treatments recommended by their 
providers. It is important to highlight that for every denied request that was eventually 
overturned, there is an actual human being whose care was unnecessarily delayed, 
potentially causing significant consequences to their health. CMS must ensure that 
patients are equipped with tools like a clear, plain language appeals process for 
instances in which delays or denials may be harmful or otherwise keep patients 
from the services, medications, and other treatments their providers recommend. 
It is also imperative that providers have as much time as possible to focus their 
attention primarily on their patients and not on paperwork. We encourage the

agency to continue to look for solutions that minimize this disruption in patient 
care.  
 
ADA Support for the Proposed Rule 
 
The ADA supports efforts CMS has taken in recent years to automate and streamline 
prior authorization processesâ€” including the most recent announcement to adding 
electronic prior authorization to the Health Tech Ecosystem.4 We have heard from many 
providers who care for patients with diabetes about the complexity and the overall 
burden associated with navigating prior authorization processes. The additional time 
and resources required to obtain prior authorization approvals detract from the time that 
providers can, and should, dedicate to caring for patients.  
 
We specifically appreciated that CMS finalized the Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization rule in 2024. 5 After this rule was finalized, we urged CMS to extend the 
application of these requirements to drugs, as we believe it is it is important that the 
enhancements to prior authorization processes and refined timelines for responding to 
prior authorization requests included in the 2024 final rule apply to drugs in addition to 
health care services so that patients can get timely access to necessary medications. 
Thus, we thank CMS for being proactive and making such a proposal now. We urge 
CMS to finalize its proposals in the proposed rule that would require select payers to:  
 
â€¢ 
Incorporate coverage and documentation requirements into Prior Authorization 
Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to support the use of electronic prior 
authorizations for drugs covered under a medical benefit  
â€¢ 
Provide a clear reason for drug prior authorization denials.  
â€¢ 
Respond to prior authorization requests under specific timeframes.  
â€¢ 
Publicly report new and revised metrics on prior authorization approvals, denials, 
and appeals for both drugs and non-drug items and services. 
We do note that many of the proposals in the rule do not apply to drugs covered under 
Medicare Part D, as CMS points out that there are existing standards and requirements 
in place for these drugs. We urge CMS to ensure that prior authorization requirements 
and standards are aligned for all drugs under Medicare to the extent possible, as many 
beneficiaries may be unaware of whether the drugs they typically receive are covered 
under Medicare Part B or Part D, and it could cause some confusion if the same prior 
authorization processes did not apply for all Medicare-covered drugs.  
 
4 CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. â€œMoving Prior Authorization into the 21st Century.â€ May 5, 2026. 
https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/blog/moving-prior-authorization-21st-century.  
5 Fed Reg. Vol. 89. Feb. 8. 2024. 8758. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-02-08/pdf/2024-00895.pdf

Arlington, VA 22202

ADA Request for CMS to Engage in Further Rulemaking to Limit the Use of Prior 
Authorization 
 
While we are supportive of the proposals to streamline prior authorization for drugs 
included in this proposed rule, we urge CMS to go further in subsequent rulemaking to 
reduce the number of services and medications that are actually subject to prior 
authorization. Further, CMS could do even more to existing streamline processes. If 
patients have already received certain treatments or medications, then there should be 
near-automatic approval processes allowedâ€”faster that the timeframes included both in 
the 2024 final rule and this proposed rule.  
 
Many individuals with chronic diseases such as diabetes rely on ongoing treatments 
and medications to help manage their conditions. However, we have heard from 
patients that they consistently have to receive approval for these services and 
medications when they continue to be the best treatment options. There is simply no 
reason for this practice. Some chronic diseases, like diabetes, can last a lifetime. 
Forcing individuals with diabetes to have to periodically re-certify that they still have 
diabetes to continue receiving a specific service or medication is not only unnecessary, 
but also adds a significant amount of burden to patients and their families and 
providersâ€”which can wind up jeopardizing access to treatment and delaying necessary 
care.  
 
ADA Response to Step Therapy Request for Information  
 
The ADA greatly appreciates that CMS requested information in the proposed rule on 
ways to streamline the step therapy process through technology and data sharing. We 
continue to have significant concerns about the use of step therapy. Also known as "fail 
first," step therapy requires patients to try a specified drug first, often a generic, less 
expensive drug, before a patient can try the medication they have been prescribed. In 
some cases, health plans require patients to fail multiple treatments before being 
approved for the drug their physician originally recommended.  
 
While CMS seeks comment on how technology may facilitate step therapy determinations 
and improve current step therapy processes, the ADA generally opposes the use of step 
therapy by Medicare Advantage (MA) plans for medications, including insulin, used for 
the treatment of diabetes. CMS has acted in the past to prohibit and limit step therapy for 
certain Part B drugs. In 2012, CMS issued a memo, Prohibition on Imposing Mandatory 
Step Therapy for Access to Part B Drugs and Services6, prohibiting MA plans from 
enacting mandatory step therapy policies for Part B drugs and services, unless already 
required through traditional Medicare. However, in 2018, CMS rescinded this memo and 
 
6 The memo is available at: https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/document/prohibition-imposing-mandatory-
step-therapy-access-part-b-drugs-and-services.  
 
 
2451 Crystal Drive, Suite 900 
 
 
Arlington, VA 22202 
1-800-DIABETES (800-342-2383) 
 
 
permitted MA plans to enact step therapy for Part B drugs. In the 2019 Modernizing Part 
D and Medicare Advantage to Lower Drug Prices and Reduce Out-of-Pocket Expenses 
final rule7, CMS enacted some step therapy oversight and imposed three limitations to 
Part B step therapy protocols: (1) step therapy can only apply to new administrations of 
a Part B drug, (2) can only include covered drugs, and (3) can include off-label products 
use only if their use is widely recognized.  
 
To best protect patients, CMS should return to its previous position of prohibiting 
step therapy in MA for Part B drugs, unless also required through traditional 
Medicare, and should prohibit step therapy use by Part D plans. If CMS chooses not 
to do that, it should further regulate step therapy for Part B and D drugs to ensure that 
patients are able to receive the medications they need in a timely way. For example, CMS 
could add explicit and required exceptions into regulation, such as if a drug could cause 
an adverse reaction, if a drug is contraindicated, or if a drug is in shortage. CMS should 
also consider an explicit exemption for medications that treat diabetes, as they have for 
antiretrovirals in Part D, due to the known harm that step therapy can have on patients 
with diabetes. 
 
Conclusion 
 
The ADA appreciates the opportunity to share these comments with CMS. Should you 
have any questions or seek additional information regarding these comments, please 
reach out to Abigail Smith, Sr. Director of Policy and Strategy at asmith@diabetes.org.  
Sincerely,  
 
Lisa Murdock 
Chief Advocacy Officer

Expenses. 84 FR. 23832 (May 23, 2019).
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Diabetes Association (ADA); signed by Lisa Murdock, Chief Advocacy Officer.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Nationwide nonprofit founded in 1940; represents people with diabetes and prediabetes, health care professionals, researchers, and others; authors widely followed diabetes standards of care.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ADA supports CMS's proposal to extend electronic prior authorization reforms to drugs, including medical benefit drug APIs, denial reasons, decision timeframes, and public reporting. It urges CMS to go further by reducing the number of services and medications subject to PA, aligning Medicare drug PA processes across Part B and Part D, creating near-automatic approvals for ongoing chronic disease treatment, and eliminating or strongly limiting step therapy in Medicare.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 Fed. Reg. 19890; 89 Fed. Reg. 8758; 84 Fed. Reg. 23832; CMS-0062-P.
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization APIs; electronic prior authorization; Medicare Part B and Part D standards; Health Tech Ecosystem reference.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extending PA reforms to drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** People with diabetes need timely access to necessary medications, and drug PA should receive the same process improvements as other services.
- **Specific request:** Finalize proposals to incorporate drug coverage/documentation requirements into PA APIs and streamline drug PA.

**Topic 2: Denial reasons, timeframes, and metrics**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Clear denial reasons, defined timeframes, and public reporting can reduce harmful delays and increase accountability.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirements for clear denial reasons, specific response timeframes, and public metrics on approvals, denials, and appeals.

**Topic 3: Medicare Part B/Part D alignment**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Beneficiaries may not know whether a drug is covered under Part B or Part D, and inconsistent PA rules could cause confusion.
- **Specific request:** Align PA requirements and standards for all Medicare-covered drugs to the extent possible.

**Topic 4: Reduce PA use and recurring approvals**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Chronic diseases such as diabetes require ongoing treatment, and repeated recertification adds burden and jeopardizes access.
- **Specific request:** Use future rulemaking to reduce services and medications subject to PA and establish near-automatic approvals for treatments patients already receive.

**Topic 5: Step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy can delay necessary and lifesaving medications, including insulin and other diabetes treatments.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit MA step therapy for Part B drugs unless required in traditional Medicare, prohibit Part D step therapy, or at minimum add required exceptions and a diabetes medication exemption.

**Topic 6: Appeals and patient protections**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Most denied MA PA requests are not appealed even though appealed denials are frequently overturned.
- **Specific request:** Ensure patients have clear, plain-language appeal processes and tools when delays or denials may be harmful.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S21:** ADA supports medical benefit drug PA APIs and believes applying 2024 PA improvements to drugs is important for timely medication access.
- **S16:** ADA supports requiring clear reasons for drug PA denials.
- **S20/S43:** ADA supports specific PA response timeframes and urges further streamlining, including faster near-automatic approval for continuing therapy.
- **S28:** ADA urges alignment of prior authorization requirements and standards for Medicare Part B and Part D drugs to avoid beneficiary confusion.
- **S29/S35:** ADA supports public reporting of approvals, denials, and appeals for drugs and non-drug items/services.
- **S66-S82:** ADA responds to the step therapy RFI by opposing step therapy for diabetes medications and urging prohibition or explicit exceptions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize drug PA API, denial reason, timeframe, and reporting proposals.
2. Align PA requirements and standards for all Medicare-covered drugs to the extent possible.
3. Pursue further rulemaking to reduce the number of services and medications subject to PA.
4. Establish near-automatic approvals for ongoing treatments or medications already received by patients.
5. Provide clear, plain-language appeal processes for harmful denials or delays.
6. Return to prohibiting mandatory MA step therapy for Part B drugs unless required in traditional Medicare.
7. Prohibit step therapy by Part D plans, or impose stronger exceptions.
8. Add step therapy exceptions for adverse reaction, contraindication, drug shortage, and diabetes medications.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Prior authorization and step therapy delay necessary care; inconsistent payer criteria; low appeal rates; repeated approvals for chronic disease therapy; and inconsistent Part B/Part D processes.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Irreparable harm, disease progression, delayed or inhibited access to lifesaving treatments, patient burden, provider paperwork, and denial of vital services.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Inconsistent payer protocols, medical necessity criteria beyond federal requirements, patient inability to appeal, and recurring recertification for lifelong conditions.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ADA represents 136 million individuals with diabetes and prediabetes; KFF reported nearly 53 million MA PA requests in 2024, 4.1 million denied or partially denied, only 11.5% appealed, and 80.7% of appealed requests approved.
- **Studies or research referenced:** ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026; KFF MA prior authorization analysis; CMS 2012 step therapy memo; 2019 MA/Part D final rule.
- **Examples provided:** Insulin and diabetes medications; chronic disease treatments; patients repeatedly recertifying that they still have diabetes; Part B and Part D drug confusion.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** People with diabetes, prediabetes, and obesity; providers; Medicare Advantage plans; Part D plans; CMS; and health plans.
- **Economic implications:** Streamlining may reduce provider administrative burden; denied care and recurring PA impose patient and provider costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** ADA supports APIs and electronic processes but argues policy should also reduce unnecessary PA use.
- **Patient care impact:** High; the comment focuses on lifesaving medication access, chronic disease continuity, and preventing disease progression.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive of rule, opposed to broad PA and step therapy use
- **Tone:** Professional, urgent, patient advocacy-oriented
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We urge CMS to go further and reduce the number of services and medications subject to prior authorization and eliminate the use of step therapy in Medicare." - Context: Overarching recommendation.
2. "Patients must be protected and have avenues to push back against denied requests." - Context: Appeal protections.
3. "There is simply no reason for this practice." - Context: Criticizing repeated recertification for chronic disease therapies.
4. "CMS should return to its previous position of prohibiting step therapy in MA for Part B drugs." - Context: Step therapy recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports response timeframes and faster continuing-treatment approvals.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Repeated PA paperwork detracts from patient care.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central focus is timely access to diabetes and chronic disease medications.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Represents large populations with diabetes and prediabetes affected by access barriers.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for alignment across Medicare Part B, Part D, MA, and traditional Medicare.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Raises confusion between Part B and Part D drug coverage.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports denial reasons, public reporting, and clear appeals.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses inconsistent payer criteria and recurring PA processes.
